name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,298

entries.clue: Began to hug learner suffering from shock? (8)

indicators.note: to hug someone is to wrap your arms around them, so STARTED closes around the L

blocks.note: L = learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

annotation.surface: A nervous beginner takes a newcomer under their wing, perhaps after some fright.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark covers a definition that is a little loose: startled is a sudden jolt rather than medical shock.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym stretched slightly: to be startled is to get a sudden fright, a small shock.

entries.clue: See mother out with Tom, Dick and Harry? (9)

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, as in 'my sums are out', so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone is told to go and visit mother, taking along any old Tom, Dick and Harry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tom, Dick and Harry' usually means just anybody; here it is taken literally as three people, and the question mark flags that definition by example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the idiom names three men, and any three together form a threesome.

entries.clue: Teacher, poor sportsman for the most part? (5)

indicators.note: for the most part means mostly, so we take most of the word and lose its last letter

blocks.note: a rabbit is a hopeless player; RABBIT loses its last letter

annotation.surface: A schoolteacher is described as being, mostly, hopeless at games.
annotation.walkthrough: In British sporting slang a rabbit is a poor player, typically a tail-end cricket batsman who rarely scores.
annotation.definitionFit: The word itself is Hebrew for 'my teacher', and a rabbi's role is teaching Jewish law.

entries.clue: Shakespearean king swallowing the tough stuff (7)

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside, so LEAR takes THE within him

annotation.surface: A king from Shakespeare forces down something hard to chew.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an overcooked steak; 'as tough as old leather' is the everyday comparison it relies on.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose descriptive definition: tanned hide is the proverbial example of something tough.

entries.clue: Given drug, do physical exercise with first hint of drowsiness (5)

indicators.note: a first hint is only the slightest trace, so just the opening letter

annotation.surface: A drugged patient is urged to exercise, though already feeling drowsy.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'do' as a verb in an instruction, but the word goes into the answer exactly as printed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: past participle for past participle, as an athlete or racehorse is doped.

entries.clue: Bishop introducing a church composer of cantatas (4)

indicators.note: to introduce is to lead something in, so B comes first

annotation.surface: A bishop presents a church musician to his congregation.
annotation.walkthrough: Bach wrote over two hundred church cantatas, so the surface's church setting is his real one.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: Johann Sebastian Bach wrote the best-known body of cantatas.

entries.clue: Group together book and sporting implement (7)

annotation.surface: Someone groups a book with a tennis racket, perhaps packing for a holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Group together' reads as an instruction to the solver to combine the pieces; it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from the punctuation mark: what sits inside brackets is set apart as one group.

entries.clue: Rod you found in church (3)

indicators.note: something found in a place is located inside it, so U sits within CE

annotation.surface: A rod you would come across in a church, perhaps a verger's staff.
annotation.walkthrough: Church can give CH or CE; only CE leaves room for a three-letter answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific example: the long tapered rod used to strike the ball in snooker and billiards.

entries.clue: Artist crushed by a black horse (4)

indicators.note: something crushed by two things is squeezed between them, so RA is pressed between A and B

annotation.surface: A painter is flattened by a dark horse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A black horse' reads as one phrase, but the definition is only 'horse'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the Arab, or Arabian, is a breed of horse.

entries.clue: Set of characters needing help by mountain height (8)

indicators.note: by means next to, so help is placed alongside, after, mountain height

annotation.surface: A group of people need assistance getting up a lofty peak.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set of characters' sounds like a cast of people; it is letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Characters here are written symbols, and an alphabet is the full set of them for a language.

entries.clue: Beautiful fairy — she had died (8)

blocks.note: a peri is a beautiful fairy of Persian myth

annotation.surface: An obituary notice for a lovely fairy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'She had' is contracted to SHE'D, dropping the apostrophe; 'had died' tempts as the definition, but only 'died' is.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both past tense: to perish is to die, especially suddenly or violently.

entries.clue: Garment left in sporting equipment? (4)

indicators.note: in means inside, so L is placed within KIT

annotation.surface: A piece of clothing has been left behind in someone's sports bag.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark hints that a kilt is itself worn at sporting events such as Highland games.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the kilt is a pleated Scottish skirt-like garment.

entries.clue: Picture of place with sand blowing around (9)

indicators.note: things blowing around in the wind are scattered, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A painting of a beach or desert with sand swirling in the wind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' is part of the fodder, joining PLACE to SAND, and the surface's windblown desert is itself a landscape.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a landscape is a picture of natural scenery.

entries.clue: Activity needing footwear with revolutionary elements (6,7)

definitions.text: Activity needing footwear with revolutionary elements

blocks.note: reads as any sport played in special shoes; the setter means one done in skates
the surface pushes rebels; the setter means wheels, rollers that go round and round

annotation.surface: A pastime whose gear sounds politically radical.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary elements' suggests rebels; it means wheels, which revolve.
annotation.definitionFit: Roller skates are boots on wheels, and wheels are the parts that turn round and round.

entries.clue: Top room protected by the Parisian framework (7)

indicators.note: what is protected is shielded on every side, so ATTIC is enclosed by LE

blocks.note: the attic is the room at the top of a house

annotation.surface: An attic is kept safe by some framework of French design.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Parisian' is a common way to ask for a French word for 'the': LE or LA.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a lattice is an open framework of crossed strips of wood or metal.

entries.clue: Sauce in vessel, cup chipped on top (7)

indicators.note: a cup chipped at the rim has lost a bit from its top, so its first letter goes

blocks.note: a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat

annotation.surface: Gravy served in a jug, with the cup beside it chipped at the rim.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a dish, the right picture for sauce, but here it is a boat.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: ketchup is a tomato-based table sauce.

entries.clue: Provision for air conditioning in Coventry (4)

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the answer sits inside the next word

annotation.surface: A building in Coventry, an English city, is fitted for air conditioning.
annotation.walkthrough: Coventry is a city in the English Midlands; the hidden answer is its middle.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a vent is the opening that lets air flow in or out of a space.

entries.clue: Old lady finally cut hair in bed (8)

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so take the last letter of cut

blocks.note: a tress is a lock of hair

annotation.surface: An elderly woman at last has her hair trimmed while lying in bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' is slang for mother, giving MA; 'in bed' is a scene, but 'in' is only the link.
annotation.definitionFit: A part standing for the whole: the mattress is the padded part of a bed, and can serve as one.

entries.clue: Duck in fog is slightly damp (5)

indicators.note: in means inside, so the duck is placed within the fog

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, O

annotation.surface: A duck out in the fog finds its feathers a little wet.
annotation.walkthrough: Duck is a cricket score of zero, shaped like O, not the bird the surface shows.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: moist is a degree of wetness short of wet, exactly slightly damp.

entries.clue: Religious follower a celebrity that's taken right to the top (5)

indicators.text: that's taken right to the top
indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the start, so the R is moved to the front

annotation.surface: A devotee idolises a celebrity who has risen straight to the summit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right' reads as 'all the way', but it is R, the last letter of ASTAR, moved to the top.
annotation.definitionFit: A shortened name: Rasta is short for Rastafarian, a follower of the Rastafari faith from Jamaica.

entries.clue: Attractive person that’s wicked inside, very wicked (8)

indicators.note: the person is wicked on the inside, so EVIL sits within DISH

blocks.note: a dish is an attractive person

annotation.surface: A charmer who is rotten underneath the good looks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' appears twice: first as wordplay giving EVIL, then within the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A comparison with the devil: devilish describes wickedness worthy of him, hence very wicked.

entries.clue: Put right, losing first and last (3)

indicators.note: to lose the first is to drop the opening letter

annotation.surface: An instruction to fix something by trimming away both ends.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Losing first and last' looks like one instruction to strip both ends; only the first letter goes, and 'last' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun sense: 'the last' of something, as in 'to the last', is its end.

entries.clue: Thus a piano is provided for TV series (4)

annotation.surface: A piano is supplied for the set of a television show.
annotation.walkthrough: P for piano is the musical marking for soft.
annotation.definitionFit: A shortened name: soap is short for soap opera, a long-running serial drama once sponsored by soap makers.

entries.clue: Lazy one worshipped, from what we hear (4)

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound of a word, not its spelling

annotation.surface: A layabout is somehow reputed to be adored.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From what we hear' could mean hearsay; here it signals that IDOL and IDLE are pronounced alike.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone idle avoids work, which is what lazy people do.

entries.clue: Cheers father having imbibed whiskey drink (3,5)

indicators.note: to imbibe is to drink in, so father takes the whiskey inside him

blocks.note: W = whiskey in the NATO phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: Dad raises a glass after downing a whisky.
annotation.walkthrough: Whiskey gives W from the radio alphabet; 'cheers' is the British informal thank-you, TA, not a toast.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: water from the tap is something you drink.
